title: Spokane Paranormal Society hunts ghosts in Hillyard's old Masonic Temple
excerpt: “What’s your husband’s name?” asks Mark Porter, co-founder of the Spokane Paranormal Society.
content:
“What’s your husband’s name?” asks Mark Porter, co-founder of the Spokane Paranormal Society.

“First name I got was Lucas,” psychic medium Amy Forness responds.

Both of them are looking directly at an empty space along the storage room wall.

We’re standing in the basement of an old Masonic Temple in Hillyard, surrounded by piles of dusty furniture, vintage sinks and scattered chandeliers stylized to be in fashion for different decades of the past.

Forness says she is speaking directly with a dead woman in a formal dress named Jocelyn, who seems to be looking for her husband, Lucas.

According to Forness, Jocelyn says a group of men wearing hats briskly took Lucas away one day. She thought they were his friends, but she hasn’t seen him since.

Forness asks if she needs help, but the deceased woman seems more confused than anything else in her mourning, which is presumably why the spirit has yet to move on to the afterlife.

A few floors above us, the old Masonic Temple hosts a beautiful ballroom in the heart of Hillyard’s historic business district. Now the Hill House Event Center, the building has maintained much of its high-society vintage charm, with high ceilings, hanging chandeliers and a custom inset bar connected to the ballroom.

But down below, the building seems to be a labyrinth that goes on forever.

Beneath the main floor, now home to the Bison Bar, the basement hides tucked-away rooms filled with enough salvaged fixtures and architectural pieces to make the place feel like a collection of several old buildings mashed together.

The concrete walls are covered in graffiti. Piles of snuffed-out cigarettes sit on the dusty floors. One room is filled with taxidermy heads, including an entire bear unsettlingly lurking in the dark. Old paintings sit near a doorway in what was once a bathroom, collecting dust next to a light-up Seattle Seahawks Bud Light sign.

In the middle of the main room, two walls are encased alongside a wide variety of carved cabinets. When I take a step closer, I notice that stapled $100 bills cover the walls from head to toe.

Paranormal investigator and Porter’s grandson Logan Souder jokingly says he wishes the bills, which were clearly printed on standard paper, were real. Souder helps with investigations and mainly monitors activity from the base camp room, where a large screen displays feeds from around the building.

I give him a joking you wish in response before we watch Forness make her way farther into the basement.

There she finds Jocelyn.

‘YOU GOT TO PROVE IT…’

On a Saturday night in September, I followed members of the Spokane Paranormal Society through the Hillyard Masonic Temple as they investigated reports of unexplained activity.

The investigation would stretch roughly 45 hours, from Friday afternoon through Sunday morning.

The owner, Aaron Fiorini, requested the group come investigate after hearing activity himself while he was alone. 

Porter decides to sleep there alone Friday night, and once everything gets ominously quiet, activity starts to happen, he says later.   

Voices. Footsteps. Running up and down the stairs in the completely desolate building.

Saturday night is when the full investigation officially started.

The group has cameras scattered throughout the building, pointed toward balconies and various points around the ballroom. One of the cameras is a structured light sensor, or SLS, camera, which picks up heat signatures and translates them into stick-like figures on a screen.

But this isn’t like a ghost show on TV. 

Before the group decides something in the building is paranormal, they spend a lot of time debunking and retracing what could have caused any activity they experience.

“I believe in it, but you got to prove it to me first,” says Brian Goldberg, one of the group’s videographers.

Goldberg considers himself one of the team’s skeptics, along with director Christine Ribble.

“Not every bump or every scrape is a ghost,” Porter adds.

An orb caught on camera could be dust. A motion sensor could have been triggered by an investigator. A noise in a wall could be a pest.

Even the equipment designed to find spirits isn’t foolproof.

Investigators know sometimes objects between the camera and its background can create false figure readings on SLS cameras. 

They also use regular camcorders, static cameras, electromagnetic field (EMF) detectors, radiating electromagnetism (REM) pods and Ovilus devices, alongside phone apps that take the place of a spirit box.

It’s basically all the stuff you might see on a ghost-hunting show, without the dramatics.

OLD BUILDINGS TELL STORIES 

The Spokane Paranormal Society was founded in 2015 by Porter and his co-founder, Ray Lusk, after the two became interested in paranormal investigation through shows like Ghost Hunters.

Their first investigation was at the Buchanan Building in downtown Spokane, built in 1911 as a funeral home and mortuary. They showed up with a K2 EMF meter to measure electromagnetic fields, a hunting camera, and a flashlight, and they spent the night talking to whatever might be there.

More than a decade later, the group has investigated locations throughout Washington, North Idaho, Montana and British Columbia.

The team of nine includes investigators, videographers, historians, directors and Forness, the in-house psychic medium, who joined about two years ago.

Forness became interested in the paranormal after having unexplained experiences as a child and into adulthood. During an underground paranormal tour in Seattle, she says her EMF meter, flashlight and recorder vest all stopped working despite having fresh batteries.

She later found the Spokane Paranormal Society through Facebook and was quickly welcomed after she showcased her skills. 

The group makes a point of not telling Forness where they’re going until immediately before an investigation so she can’t research the location ahead of time.

“We call her the mushroom because we keep her in the dark,” says Tammy Pounds, the group’s director of operations.

Forness’ role is different from a medium who reads people.

“Mine is more of properties, like buildings, areas, the land,” she says.

Sometimes, she says, she can get visions before arriving at a location. The group will then research whether the findings match anything in the building’s history.

Pounds and Ribble, the group’s resident historians, dig through the Northwest Room at the Spokane Public Library, searching old newspapers and magazines, online records and information from property owners.

The Spokane Valley Museum has also helped them track down historical material that isn’t available elsewhere.

Sometimes that research lines up almost perfectly with what Forness experiences on-site.

“My favorite was at the Lake City Playhouse,” Pounds says. “We had a girl who was murdered on the way home from a dance. And [Amy] picked up on it, and she’s like describing the dress and describing the girl, and it was just on the nose to what my research was.”

‘HIGHLY  METAPHYSICAL…’

The Masonic Temple has plenty of its own history for the group to dig through. Built in 1931, the second floor served as the Masonic Temple, while the lower portions of the building have housed businesses over the years, including a grocery store and even a J.C. Penney.

The group has investigated several other Hillyard locations, too, including Market Street Antiques, the Bad Seed and Hillyard Variety antique store.

Forness calls the old Masonic building a “Grand Central Station in Hillyard” for spirits, a place she describes as massively haunted.

Based on their experiences investigating around Hillyard, Porter and Forness believe the neighborhood is connected by what they describe as an “underground” of spirits moving between locations.

For the group, investigating isn’t just about finding spirits. It’s also about figuring out whether they can help them move on.

“We have a lady who stares backwards out of Market Street Antiques still waiting for her fiance to come back from World War II, but he died there and they never told her because she wasn’t his wife,” Porter says. “So she’s still staring out that back window, and we can’t convince her to go.”

For negative entities, moving them along can get a little more intense.

At the Masonic Temple, Porter says the group encountered six spirits and one negative entity.

He wouldn’t call it a demon, but believed it could have become something more harmful before they cleaned it up. 

Forness described it as being “like smoke.”

Porter is a nondenominational Christian and says many members of the group were raised Christian, although everyone has their own approach, adding that sometimes they “ask God, Jesus, the Holy Spirit to send in the archangel Michael.”

For spirits that the group believes are ready to cross over, like Jocelyn, Porter describes creating a sphere of light and opening a door within it, where a loved one from the other side can greet the spirit.

“Highly metaphysical stuff and nothing that we could prove beyond a shadow of a doubt, but that’s just what we’ve seen in my 11 years of doing this,” he says.

One of Porter’s most memorable experiences happened at the Old Montana State Penitentiary in Deer Lodge, Montana. The group was locked inside overnight while investigating a tower associated with an explosive 1959 riot.

While walking down the stairs, Porter says he felt something odd scrape across his shoulder. A member of the group took a look and found three distinctive scratch marks.

A correspondent from a Butte ABC affiliate was there that night and photographed the marks, Porter says. She had planned to stay with the group all night but left shortly after the encounter.

Porter says he’s experienced other physical sensations during investigations, including being scratched, punched and touched.

Back at the Masonic Temple, we can’t see what, or who, Forness is talking to. But in a building this old, with many rooms, stories and people who have passed through, there is certainly no shortage of energy left behind.
